rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier
rows.stem: Give two differences between a half wave rectifier and a full wave rectifier.
rows.solution:
| | Half-wave rectifier | Full-wave rectifier |
|---|---|---|
| **Which half-cycles are used** | Only one half of each input cycle; the other half is discarded | **Both** halves are used, the reverse half being inverted rather than thrown away |
| **Output frequency** | The **same** as the input frequency | **Twice** the input frequency |
| **Diodes needed** | One | Two, with a centre-tapped transformer (or four in a bridge) |
| **Average dc output** | \(\dfrac{V_m}{\pi}\) | \(\dfrac{2V_m}{\pi}\) — twice as large |
| **Efficiency** | About \(40{\cdot}6\%\) at best | About \(81{\cdot}2\%\) |
| **Ripple** | Large, with long gaps between pulses | Smaller, and easier still to smooth because the gaps are shorter |

Any two of these answer the question; the first two are the ones that matter most.

**Why the doubled frequency is the important difference.** It is not simply a curiosity of the waveform — it is what makes the full-wave rectifier so much easier to filter. The output is smoothed by a capacitor across the load, and the capacitor must hold the voltage up during the gap between pulses. At twice the frequency that gap is half as long, so the same capacitor produces a far steadier dc.

Combine that with the doubled average output and the picture is clear: a half-wave rectifier wastes half the input and delivers a pulsating output that is hard to smooth, which is why real power supplies are full-wave.

rows.subtopic: Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem:
An electron in a hydrogen atom makes transitions from orbits of higher energies to orbits of lower energies.
(i) When will such transitions result in (a) Lyman (b) Balmer series ?
(ii) Find the ratio of the longest wavelength in Lyman series to the shortest wavelength in Balmer series.
rows.solution:
**(i) When each series is produced.**

A spectral series is named for the level the electron **lands on**, not the one it leaves.

**Lyman series** — the electron falls to \(n_f = 1\), the ground state, from any higher orbit \(n_i = 2, 3, 4, \ldots \infty\). These photons are the most energetic of all hydrogen's lines and lie in the **ultraviolet**.

**Balmer series** — the electron falls to \(n_f = 2\), from \(n_i = 3, 4, 5, \ldots \infty\). These lie mostly in the **visible**, and are the only hydrogen lines the eye can see.

**(ii) The ratio.**

Use \(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)\) twice.

**Longest wavelength in the Lyman series** — the *smallest* energy jump that ends on \(n = 1\), which is \(n_i = 2\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_1} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{1^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{2^{2}}\right) = R\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{3R}{4}\)

\(\lambda_1 = \dfrac{4}{3R}\)

**Shortest wavelength in the Balmer series** — the *largest* jump ending on \(n = 2\), the series limit at \(n_i = \infty\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_2} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{2^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right) = \dfrac{R}{4}\)

\(\lambda_2 = \dfrac{4}{R}\)

**The ratio:**

\(\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{4/3R}{4/R} = \dfrac{1}{3}\)

\(\lambda_1 : \lambda_2 = 1 : 3\)

The Rydberg constant cancels, so the answer is a pure number.

**A check worth making.** \(\lambda_1 \approx 1216\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(\lambda_2 \approx 3646\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\), and \(3646/1216 \approx 3\). Both are ultraviolet, which is the point of the comparison: even the *shortest* Balmer wavelength is three times the *longest* Lyman one, so **the two series do not overlap at all** — every Lyman line is more energetic than every Balmer line. That is a general feature, and it is why hydrogen's spectrum separates cleanly into series.

rows.stem: With the help of a ray diagram, show how a compound microscope forms a magnified image of a tiny object, at least distance of distinct vision. Hence derive an expression for the magnification produced by it.
rows.solution:
**The instrument.** Two converging lenses on a common axis: an **objective** of short focal length \(f_o\) facing the object, and an **eyepiece** of focal length \(f_e\) at the other end of a tube of length \(L\).

**The ray diagram, described.**

The tiny object AB is placed just **beyond** the objective's focus, so \(f_o < u < 2f_o\). The objective forms a **real, inverted and enlarged** image \(\mathrm{A'B'}\) inside the tube.

That first image is then positioned just **inside** the focal length of the eyepiece, so the eyepiece acts as a simple magnifier on it. It forms a **virtual, further enlarged** final image \(\mathrm{A''B''}\) on the same side as \(\mathrm{A'B'}\), at the **least distance of distinct vision \(D\)** (25 cm) from the eye. The final image is inverted with respect to the original object.

Draw two rays from the top of the object through the objective to locate \(\mathrm{A'B'}\), then two from the top of \(\mathrm{A'B'}\) through the eyepiece, and project the emergent rays backwards as dashed lines to meet at \(\mathrm{A''}\).

**Deriving the magnification.**

The two lenses act in succession, so the magnifications **multiply**:

\(m = m_o \times m_e\)

*The objective.* Its linear magnification is the ratio of image size to object size:

\(m_o = \dfrac{h'}{h}\)

The first image is formed close to the eyepiece's focal plane, so its distance from the objective is very nearly the tube length \(L\), while the object sits almost at the objective's focus. From similar triangles about the objective (the ray through its centre subtends the same angle \(\beta\) on both sides),

\(\tan\beta = \dfrac{h}{f_o} = \dfrac{h'}{L}\)

\(m_o = \dfrac{h'}{h} = \dfrac{L}{f_o}\)

*The eyepiece.* Used as a simple microscope with the final image at \(D\), its magnification is the standard result

\(m_e = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\)

*Total.*

\(m = \dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right)\)

**What the expression says.** Both focal lengths appear in **denominators**, so a powerful microscope needs *both* lenses short — and the objective's \(f_o\) matters most, since it enters directly rather than through the "\(1 +\)". A long tube helps as well, which is why microscopes are tall.

Note also the contrast with the relaxed-eye setting. If the final image is instead formed at infinity, \(m_e = D/f_e\) and the total magnification is smaller by the term \(L/f_o\). The arrangement asked for here — image at \(D\) — gives the **largest** magnification the instrument can produce, at the cost of some eye strain.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem:
(a) Give an example each of a metal from which photoelectric emission takes place when irradiated by (i) UV light (ii) visible light.
(b) The work function of a metal is 4.50 eV. Find the frequency of light to be used to eject electrons from the metal surface with a maximum kinetic energy of \(6.06\times10^{-19}\mathrm{J}\).
rows.solution:
**(a) One metal for each.**

**(i) Ultraviolet light: zinc.** (Magnesium or cadmium serve equally well.) Zinc has a work function of about \(4{\cdot}3\) eV, so its threshold wavelength is roughly \(2900\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) — well into the ultraviolet. Visible light, however bright, frees no electrons from zinc; the classic demonstration is a zinc plate on an electroscope that discharges under a mercury lamp and not under a filament bulb.

**(ii) Visible light: caesium.** (Sodium, potassium or lithium also work.) The alkali metals have the lowest work functions of all — caesium's is about \(2{\cdot}1\) eV, sodium's \(2{\cdot}3\) eV — putting their thresholds at roughly \(5800\) and \(5400\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\), inside the visible range. This is why photocell cathodes are coated with caesium.

The pattern is not an accident: the alkali metals hold their single outer electron most loosely, so the least energy is needed to remove it.

**(b) The frequency required.**

Einstein's photoelectric equation:

\(h\nu = \phi_0 + K_{\max}\)

Convert the work function to joules so that both terms share units:

\(\phi_0 = 4{\cdot}50\ \mathrm{eV} = 4{\cdot}50 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} = 7{\cdot}20 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

Then

\(h\nu = 7{\cdot}20 \times 10^{-19} + 6{\cdot}06 \times 10^{-19} = 13{\cdot}26 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(\nu = \dfrac{13{\cdot}26 \times 10^{-19}}{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}\)

\(\nu = 2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{15}\ \mathrm{Hz}\)

**Orientation.** That corresponds to \(\lambda = c/\nu = 1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(= 1500\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\), far ultraviolet — which makes sense, since the photon must carry \(8{\cdot}3\) eV in total. The threshold for this metal alone would be \(\nu_0 = \phi_0/h \approx 1{\cdot}1 \times 10^{15}\) Hz, so the light used is nearly twice the threshold frequency.

**A caution about the arithmetic.** The work function is given in electronvolts and the kinetic energy in joules. Adding them as printed would be meaningless; one must be converted before the other is touched. Mixing the two units is the commonest way to lose this question, and it produces an answer wrong by a factor of \(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\) rather than a small slip.
